description:
Immediately beside Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque, on the spot where Maharaja Ranjit Singh's body was cremated, stands the samadhi built in his memory — one of the grandest funerary monuments of the Sikh Empire. Ranjit Singh, the "Lion of Punjab," founded and ruled the Sikh Empire from 1801 until his death on 27 June 1839. Construction began the following month under his son Kharak Singh and was largely completed by 1848 under his youngest son, Duleep Singh, with final repairs funded by the British after their 1849 annexation of Punjab. At the monument's heart, beneath a marble pavilion inlaid with pietra dura stonework, a lotus-shaped marble urn holds the Maharaja's ashes, surrounded by smaller urns commemorating the four queens and seven attendants who, according to the custom of sati, died on his funeral pyre. Adjoining smaller samadhis honour his son Kharak Singh and grandson Nau Nihal Singh. Architecturally the building is a striking synthesis of Sikh, Hindu and Islamic idioms: gilded fluted domes and cupolas rise above red sandstone doorways carved with images of Ganesha, Devi and Brahma, while surviving interior frescoes, painted between 1839 and 1849, have been reassessed by modern scholars as a high point of Sikh decorative art. Though formally a samadhi rather than a constituted gurdwara, the site has long functioned as a living place of Sikh devotion: the Guru Granth Sahib was installed and read there for decades after construction, and today it remains an active pilgrimage destination, especially around Ranjit Singh's death anniversary and the spring Vaisakhi season, when Sikh visitors, including delegations from India, gather to pay homage. The Evacuee Trust Property Board administers the site, one of the most visited symbols of Sikh heritage remaining in Pakistan.

Modern scholarship has focused particular attention on the samadhi's ornamental programme: research by the art historian Dr Nadhra Shahbaz Naeem Khan uncovered guardian figures beneath whitewash on the building's eastern facade, though subsequent recoatings have since covered and lost this decoration again. The monument is listed by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology among the province's protected religious monuments of the Sikh period.

## Bibliography
- Bushra Shehzad, "Rediscovering our Sikh heritage," *Dawn*, 24 May 2012.
- Directorate General of Archaeology, Government of Punjab, "Religious Monuments" (online monument index), accessed 16 August 2026.
qa_note: A Dunya News feature (15 August 2026) states that "the structure originally served as a baradari where Maharaja Ranjit Singh held royal gatherings before it was converted into a memorial Samadhi" and that it "houses commemorative urns associated with the Maharaja's ashes, while tradition holds that most of his ashes were immersed in the River Ganges." Neither claim is corroborated by the two earlier, more rigorously sourced accounts drawn on above — Syad Muhammad Latif's 1892 *Lahore: Its History, Architectural Remains and Antiquities* and Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* — both of which describe the building as commissioned only after Ranjit Singh's death, as a mausoleum begun under his son Kharak Singh, and both describe the marble lotus in the central vault as directly covering the Maharaja's ashes on-site, with no mention of a Ganges immersion. This discrepancy is reported here, not resolved. Dunya News also gives a vaguer account of who completed construction ("subsequent Sikh rulers") than Latif's more precise sequence (begun under Kharak Singh, partly executed by Sher Singh, finished only in the later part of Dalip Singh's reign).
